title: Baba Deep Singh, 1757
hookLine: the old scholar-warrior rides to free the Harmandir; tradition says he fought on with his head in his hand

lines: A SMALL SHRINE BY THE POOL.
cards: Walk around the pool at the Golden Temple and you'll pass a small shrine where people stop, bow and whisper.
Many visitors are surprised by the painting they often see of the man it remembers: an old warrior with a long white beard, sword in one hand, his own head held in the other. It sounds like a legend.
Sikhs tell it with love and awe, and they'll also tell you why it matters more than the miracle. Today: Baba Deep Singh.

teach.b: Baba means elder, grandfather, a title of love for someone old and wise.

teach.h: THE SCHOLAR WHO COPIED THE GRANTH.
teach.b: Deep Singh was, first of all, a scholar.
Tradition says he took amrit from Guru Gobind Singh himself, and spent years at Damdama Sahib, the Guru's seat of learning, copying the Guru Granth Sahib by hand so more Sikhs could have it.
Some of those copies were sent to the takhts.

teach.h: 1757: A VOW TO FREE THE HARMANDIR.
teach.b: He was also a warrior, and by 1757 an old one, around seventy-five. That year, forces of the Afghan king Ahmad Shah Abdali occupied Amritsar and desecrated the Harmandir.
When the news reached Damdama Sahib, Baba Deep Singh made a vow: he would go to Amritsar and free it, or die trying. Riders joined him along the way.
Tradition says he drew a line on the ground and asked only those ready to give their lives to cross it. The Afghan army met them a few miles from Amritsar, and the fighting was fierce.

teach.h: THE ACCOUNTS DIFFER; THE VOW HELD.
teach.b: Here the accounts differ. The best-known tradition says his head was struck off, and he held it on his palm and fought on until he reached the sacred precinct, and laid it there.
Other accounts say he was mortally wounded in the neck and fought on to the end. Either way, he finished what he'd vowed.

Sikhs find the image powerful because it pictures a promise that outlasts even the body. Most of us make small vows every week, and leave them half done. Baba Deep Singh is the old man who finished his.

how: Pilgrims at the Harmandir Sahib stop at the place in the parikrama where tradition says Baba Deep Singh fell, and Gurdwara Shaheedan in Amritsar honors him and his companions; his birthday and martyrdom are marked each year.

games.q: you're around seventy-five, a scholar at Damdama Sahib. news comes that the Harmandir has been desecrated. what do you do?
o: vow to free it or die trying, and ride.
stay with your books; you're too old.
games.why: Baba Deep Singh made the vow and rode to Amritsar. tradition says he finished it even past death.

practice: Think of something you started and left undone that still matters: a book half read, a message half written, a promise to call someone, a project in a drawer. Picture it finished, how it looks and how it feels.
Then settle on the very next step, small enough for today, and let that decision rest in your body.

wordCard.voice: Baba. Elder, grandfather, a title of love — given to the old scholar-warrior who vowed to free the Harmandir in 1757 and, tradition says, fought on until he reached it.

carryVoice: Your line: finish the vow. Even the half-done ones. That's day two hundred ninety.
